questions.stem: Simple covalent molecules like methane (CH₄) have low boiling points. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: The covalent bonds within the molecules are weak and easy to break
The intermolecular forces between molecules are weak and require little energy to overcome
The molecules have very few electrons
The molecules are very light

questions.explanation: When simple covalent substances boil, it is the weak intermolecular forces (forces between molecules) that are overcome, NOT the strong covalent bonds within the molecules. The covalent bonds remain intact. A very common exam mistake is to say the covalent bonds break - they do not. The molecules separate from each other.

questions.stem: Why do simple covalent molecules not conduct electricity?

options.text: They contain too few atoms
They have no free electrons or ions to carry charge
Their bonds are too strong
They are always gases at room temperature

questions.explanation: Simple covalent molecules have no free electrons (all electrons are in shared pairs) and no ions. Without charged particles that are free to move, they cannot conduct electricity. This applies in any state - solid, liquid, or gas. Some simple molecular substances like water are liquids at room temperature.

questions.stem: A student says: 'When water boils at 100°C, the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen break.' Is this correct?

options.text: Yes, the bonds break to release hydrogen and oxygen gases
Yes, but only some of the bonds break
No, only the intermolecular forces between water molecules are overcome; the H-O bonds remain intact
No, water cannot boil because the bonds are too strong

questions.explanation: When water boils, the intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are overcome, allowing molecules to escape as steam. The covalent O-H bonds within each water molecule remain intact. The steam still consists of H₂O molecules. Breaking O-H bonds would require much more energy and would decompose water into hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.stem: Substance X is a liquid at room temperature, does not conduct electricity, and has a boiling point of 78°C. What type of structure does it most likely have?

options.text: Giant ionic lattice
Giant covalent structure
Simple covalent (molecular)
Metallic structure

questions.explanation: The low boiling point (78°C) and lack of electrical conductivity are characteristic of a simple covalent (molecular) substance. Giant ionic lattices have high melting points and conduct when dissolved. Giant covalent structures have very high melting points. Metals conduct electricity. This substance is likely ethanol.

questions.stem: As the size of simple covalent molecules increases, what generally happens to their boiling points?

options.text: Boiling points decrease because larger molecules are less stable
Boiling points stay the same because covalent bonds are equally strong
Boiling points increase because intermolecular forces become stronger with more electrons
Boiling points increase because the covalent bonds get stronger

questions.explanation: Larger molecules have more electrons, which leads to stronger London dispersion forces (a type of intermolecular force) between molecules. Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to overcome, resulting in higher boiling points. The strength of the covalent bonds within molecules is not the relevant factor for boiling points.
